en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga.
9. The Somanassa Jātaka “Who harms you or oppresses you?
Why are you dejected, grieving, and ill at ease?”
"Today let the parents weep;
where on earth has the bridge been struck down today?
"I am glad, O King, at the sight of you."
"After a long time, O protector of the earth, I behold you.
Having entered the dust as one who practices non-violence,
I have been struck down by your son, O King."
“Let the gatekeepers with their swords girded come forward;
let the followers of Kāśyapa enter the inner palace!
Having slain that Prince Somanassa, [let them depart].”
“Having cut off his head, bring it here.
Sent by the king,
the messengers spoke thus to the prince:
“You have been abandoned by the Lord;
you have met with death, O Kṣatriya.
Thus the prince lamented.
Raising my ten fingers in the añjali gesture,
O Lord of Men, I too wish to see you;
having brought me back alive, please show yourself to me.
Having heard those words of his,
they showed him the king’s son;
and the son, seeing his father, [rejoiced].
"Speak from afar! O King,
let the gatekeepers, girt with swords and clad in saffron robes, slay me!"
"Being asked, tell me this matter:
what fault indeed do I have here today?
"I sprinkle water in the evening and in the morning."
“He is always devoted to tending the fire;
why do you call such a self-controlled practitioner of the holy life a ‘householder’?”
“O King, his various possessions consist of palm trees, roots, and fruits;
he protects and guards them with great diligence.”
"Therefore, I say, 'Householder.
'What you say is indeed true, young man;
there are various kinds of possessions belonging to him.'"
He guards and protects them with diligence;
by that, he is a brahmin or a householder.
"Let my assembled assembly listen to me."
The people of Sānegama and all the inhabitants of the countryside,
having listened to the words of this fool,
have caused me to be executed by the lord of men for no reason at all.
When its roots are firm, spread out, and grown large,
the bamboo that has produced side-shoots is indeed difficult to uproot;
O Lord of Men, I pay homage at your feet.
“Give me your permission, O King, I shall go forth.
“Enjoy vast wealth, O Prince,
and I grant you all sovereignty.”
“Become the king of the Kurus this very day;
do not go forth into homelessness, for the life of a renunciant is suffering.
“What wealth, O King, do you have here?”
I shall dwell in the world of the gods,
enjoying forms, sounds, and likewise tastes,
scents, and touches that are delightful to the mind.
I enjoyed pleasures in the world of the Thirty-three gods,
surrounded by a host of nymphs; yet,
knowing you to be a fool who follows the lead of others, I departed.
“I would not dwell in such a royal household.
“If I am a fool and led by others,
my son, forgive me for this one transgression.”
If such a thing should happen again,
act with joy according to your own judgment.
“Action performed without reflection...”
Thought that is not firmly established is like the dissolution of medicine;
its result is evil.
Action performed with reflection and intended for a proper foundation brings success,
just like the efficacy of medicine.
The ripening is auspicious.
A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good;
one who has gone forth but is unrestrained is not good.
It is not good for a king to act without reflection;
it is not good for one who is wise to be angry.
A kshatriya should act with reflection.
Not by lack of reflection does one become a lord of the earth;
O King, for those who act with circumspection,
glory and fame increase.
A lord should mete out punishment with careful consideration;
a ruler of the earth who acts with haste suffers remorse;
and for a man, well-directed intentions lead to his welfare.
They have no regrets later on.
For those who perform actions in this world that are free from regret, having analyzed the spheres of action;
Those things praised by the wise,
which result in happiness, are approved by the Buddhas.
Then the gatekeepers, girded with swords, arrived.
"O Lord of Men, let the Kāsāviyas kill me! O King,
while I was sitting on my mother's lap,
I was suddenly dragged away by them."
For I have reached a sharp and painful strait,
O King, though I have obtained a life that is sweet;
today, through hardship, I have been released from execution.
“I am one who truly delights in going forth.
“This young son of yours, O Sudhamma,
is a compassionate and joyful prince;”
“Though I entreated him for it, I did not obtain it today;
you too ought to entreat him for it.
“Delight, my son, in the practice of wandering for alms.”
Reflecting deeply upon all phenomena, go forth as a wanderer;
laying aside the rod toward all living beings,
blameless, attain the state of Brahmā.
“Truly, it is a wondrous thing that you, who are well-established in the Dhamma,
should cause me, who am already suffering, to suffer even more!
Though addressed thus, ‘Ask for a son,’”
“You further encourage the prince.
“Those who are fully liberated, who enjoy blameless wealth,
and who wander this world having attained final Nibbāna;”
“I cannot restrain the prince as he proceeds upon that path leading to the deathless.
“Truly, those possessed of wisdom must certainly be served;”
Those who are learned and contemplate many points,
who, having heard these well-spoken words,
become free from anxiety, devoid of sorrow, and established in the True Dhamma.
The Ninth Jātaka: Somanassa.
